title: Trump: U.S. Supreme Court rules that corporations have human rights
description_short: Trump: U.S. Supreme Court rules that corporations have human rights
description_medium: TrumpFile’s page presents the Supreme Court’s 2014 Burwell v. Hobby Lobby decision as granting corporations religious-freedom protections and compares those protections to individual rights. The case-specific account supplied for this record concerns closely held companies seeking a Religious Freedom Restoration Act exemption from the contraceptive-coverage rule. The TrumpFile page does not identify a Trump statement or action connected to the decision.
description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline entry, dated June 30, 2014, reports the Supreme Court’s decision in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby and characterizes it as recognizing corporate religious-freedom protections. The page goes further, asserting that corporations consequently have the same rights as natural persons and might have more rights than individuals. The case-specific account supplied with this record describes a narrower holding: closely held for-profit corporations could bring a claim under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act against the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive-coverage requirement. That is not a general declaration that corporations possess every human right. The difference matters because the page’s headline and argument broaden a defined statutory ruling. The linked TrumpFile entry identifies the 2014 case but does not document a Trump statement, appointment, policy, or other action tying him to the decision. The material supports describing the page’s characterization and the narrower legal issue, but it does not establish a Trump-specific event. A source connecting Trump to the ruling or documenting the statement attributed to him is still needed.

title: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
description_short: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
description_medium: TrumpFile reports that Eric Trump appeared on Fox News with Jeanine Pirro and called the pandemic a hoax, saying stay-at-home orders were intended to hurt his father rather than protect people from rising COVID-19 cases. The page also says Pirro added a claim about Democrats and election-day voting. TrumpFile displays May 16, 2020, while the assigned record is dated May 17.
description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline entry says Eric Trump appeared on Fox News host Jeanine Pirro’s program and described the COVID-19 pandemic as a hoax. It attributes to him the claim that state stay-at-home orders were intended to hurt Donald Trump rather than respond to rising cases. The page says Pirro did not challenge that claim and added her own claim that Democrats wanted to make voters afraid to vote on Election Day. These are statements attributed to Eric Trump and Pirro, not facts about the pandemic or the purpose of public-health orders. The page’s displayed date is May 16, 2020, whereas the assignment record is dated May 17, 2020. The linked page confirms the comments but does not identify a separate broadcast date or explain the one-day discrepancy. The source date could reflect publication rather than the date of the interview, but that distinction is not established here. The event date remains unresolved until a broadcast or contemporaneous record confirms when the interview aired.

title: Trump: FCC approves illegal acquisition of TEGNA by Nexstar in big blow to local media
description_short: Trump: FCC approves illegal acquisition of TEGNA by Nexstar in big blow to local media
description_medium: TrumpFile reports that the FCC and DOJ approved the Nexstar–TEGNA merger on March 19, 2026. It says Nexstar would own 259 stations, reach 54.5% of U.S. households after divesting six stations, and faced a lawsuit from eight states. The page describes the states’ claim that the deal violated federal reach limits, but reports no final court ruling on legality.
description_long: On March 19, 2026, TrumpFile reported that the FCC and Justice Department had approved Nexstar’s merger with TEGNA. The page says the combined company would own 259 television stations and reach 54.5% of U.S. households after agreeing to divest six stations. It also reports that eight states sued to challenge the merger, alleging that it exceeded the 39% household-reach cap. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser warned that consolidation could reduce media diversity and raise costs; Nexstar chair and CEO Perry Sook is named in the account of the stations. These points describe regulatory approval, the stated divestitures, and a pending legal challenge. The TrumpFile page calls the transaction illegal, but it reports no final judgment establishing that conclusion. Its linked CBS News article concerns a separate FCC matter involving Disney and ABC and does not resolve this merger’s legal status. Neither linked page documents a Trump order or action behind the approval. A final ruling and a sourced Trump-specific connection remain missing for the categorical illegality and Trump framing in the record.
